Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN) -- The fiery leader of Lebanon's Hezbollah militant movement assured Lebanon on Monday that his movement will cooperate in the country's political life. Supporters carry posters of Hezbollah chief Hassan Nasrallah. Hassan Nasrallah said: "We don't want to have control over Lebanon, or to have governance over Lebanon or to impose our ideas over the people of Lebanon, because we believe Lebanon to be a special and diverse country that needs the collaboration of everyone." Nasrallah spoke a day after Lebanon's parliament elected Michel Sleiman the country's president after a six-month vacancy in the position. Nasrallah, speaking at a packed stadium, told his followers: "I renew my appeal and invitation for a true national partnership with no eliminations or impositions. The national unity government is not the victory of the opposition against the pro-government. It is the victory of all Lebanese." He said Sleiman's election "renews the hope amongst the Lebanese people to a new era and a new start." "I must say that there are deep wounds from our side and theirs, we are both in front of two choices; either to expand the wounds and add salt to them or try to cure them for the sake of Lebanon and we prefer the second choice." The parliament had tried 19 times to vote on a new president, but failed because of disagreements over how to share power in a new Cabinet. Lebanon's Western-backed government and the Hezbollah-led opposition reached a deal last week aimed at ending an 18-month political crisis that pushed the country to the brink of civil war, and paved the way for Sleiman's election. The agreement, reached in Doha, Qatar, calls for a consensus government in which the Cabinet would be comprised of 30 posts -- 16 for the majority, 11 for the Hezbollah-led opposition and three set aside for the president to nominate. The seat allocation had been a key sticking point for the opposition, which wanted to ensure it had the power to veto major decisions. With 11 Cabinet posts, it will have that power. In exchange for the veto power and a redistricting plan ahead of next year's elections, Hezbollah agreed to end its sit-in protest that has paralyzed downtown Beirut since late 2006. In his speech, Sleiman expressed gratitude to Qatar and to the Arab League for helping broker the deal. Sleiman was the consensus candidate, and is viewed as a neutral party by Lebanon's political factions. The nation's previous presidents have been seen as either pro-Syrian or pro-Western. In his 10 years as chief of the army, Sleiman also is believed to have unified the splintered military. However, he inherits a nation grappling with divisions. Lebanon's elected, pro-Western government has long been locked in a power struggle with Hezbollah. In public statements and demonstrations in recent years, Hezbollah threatened to use its power and popularity to oust the Sunni-led government, triggering fears of a new civil war that could further destabilize the volatile region. The election helped end a political crisis that deteriorated into violence this month. That crisis was defused when the Lebanese government gave in to two key Hezbollah demands -- lifting a government ban of Hezbollah's telecommunications system and reinstating the chief of security at Beirut's airport. "The performance of the opposition proved that it did not organize a coup, but only wanted the illegal government to withdraw its two decisions," Nasrallah said. "I promise that the opposition's representation in the government will not be monopolized by Hezbollah, Amal and the Change and Reform bloc. We will give other opposition parties shares - and unfortunately we must speak of shares - even if it is at the expense of Hezbollah's shares." Hezbollah has been linked to numerous terrorist attacks against U.S., Israeli, and other Western targets and the United States lists it as a terrorist organization. But many in Lebanon and other parts of the Middle East -- particularly Shiites -- view Hezbollah militants as freedom fighters.

BEIRUT, Lebanon (CNN) -- The fiery leader of Lebanon's Hezbollah militant movement assured the nation on Monday that his organization would remain committed to cooperative engagement in the country's political life. Supporters carried posters bearing the image of Hezbollah chief Hassan Nasrallah as he addressed the crowd.

"We don't want to have control over Lebanon, or to have governance over Lebanon, or to impose our ideas over the people of Lebanon," Nasrallah declared, "because we believe Lebanon to be a special and diverse country that needs the collaboration of everyone."

Nasrallah's remarks came a day after Lebanon's parliament elected Michel Sleiman as the country's president, ending a six-month vacancy in the post. Speaking before a packed stadium of supporters, Nasrallah stated: "I renew my appeal and invitation for a true national partnership with no eliminations or impositions. The national unity government is not the victory of the opposition against the pro-government. It is the victory of all Lebanese."

He characterized Sleiman's election as an event that "renews the hope amongst the Lebanese people to a new era and a new start," adding: "I must say that there are deep wounds from our side and theirs. We are both faced with two choices: either to expand the wounds and add salt to them, or to try to heal them for the sake of Lebanon. We prefer the second choice."

The parliament had attempted 19 previous votes on a new president, each failing amid disagreements over how power would be shared within a new Cabinet. Lebanon's Western-backed government and the Hezbollah-led opposition ultimately reached an accord last week aimed at resolving an 18-month political crisis that had pushed the country to the brink of civil war, thereby clearing the path for Sleiman's election.

The agreement, brokered in Doha, Qatar, established a consensus government in which the Cabinet would comprise 30 posts: 16 allocated to the majority, 11 to the Hezbollah-led opposition, and three reserved for presidential nomination. The distribution of seats had proven a central point of contention for the opposition, which sought assurance of veto power over major decisions—power it secured through its allotment of 11 Cabinet posts.

In exchange for this veto power, along with a redistricting plan ahead of next year's elections, Hezbollah agreed to end the sit-in protest that had paralyzed downtown Beirut since late 2006.

In his own address, Sleiman expressed gratitude to Qatar and the Arab League for their role in brokering the settlement. As the consensus candidate, Sleiman is regarded by Lebanon's political factions as a neutral figure—a notable distinction, given that the nation's previous presidents have typically been perceived as either pro-Syrian or pro-Western. During his decade as army chief, Sleiman is also credited with unifying a previously fractured military.

Nonetheless, he assumes the presidency of a nation still grappling with deep divisions. Lebanon's elected, pro-Western government has long been engaged in a power struggle with Hezbollah. Through public statements and demonstrations in recent years, Hezbollah has threatened to leverage its power and popularity to oust the Sunni-led government—raising fears of renewed civil war that could further destabilize an already volatile region.

The presidential election helped resolve a political crisis that had escalated into violence earlier this month. That crisis was ultimately defused when the Lebanese government acceded to two central Hezbollah demands: lifting the ban on Hezbollah's telecommunications system and reinstating the chief of security at Beirut's airport.

"The performance of the opposition proved that it did not organize a coup, but only wanted the illegal government to withdraw its two decisions," Nasrallah said. He further pledged: "I promise that the opposition's representation in the government will not be monopolized by Hezbollah, Amal, and the Change and Reform bloc. We will give other opposition parties shares—and unfortunately we must speak of shares—even if it comes at the expense of Hezbollah's own allocation."

Hezbollah has been linked to numerous terrorist attacks against American, Israeli, and other Western targets, and remains designated a terrorist organization by the United States. Yet across Lebanon and much of the Middle East—particularly among Shiite communities—many regard Hezbollah's militants not as terrorists, but as freedom fighters.

His remarks came one day after Lebanese lawmakers chose Michel Sleiman as the nation's president, filling a post that had remained empty for six months. Addressing a crowded stadium of supporters, Nasrallah declared: "I am renewing my call for genuine national partnership, free from exclusion or domination. This unity government represents no victory of the opposition over the ruling side—rather, it belongs to all Lebanese people."

He characterized Sleiman's election as something that "restores hope among Lebanese citizens for a fresh chapter and new beginnings." He continued: "I must acknowledge that both sides carry deep wounds. We now face two paths forward: deepening those wounds further, or working to heal them for Lebanon's sake. We choose healing."

Lawmakers had made 19 previous unsuccessful attempts to elect a president, repeatedly stalled by disputes over Cabinet power-sharing arrangements. Last week, an agreement between Lebanon's Western-aligned government and the Hezbollah-backed opposition brought an end to 18 months of political turmoil that had threatened to plunge the country into civil conflict, clearing the way for Sleiman's presidency.

This accord, negotiated in Doha, Qatar, establishes a unity government with 30 Cabinet positions distributed as follows: 16 seats for the majority bloc, 11 for the opposition coalition led by Hezbollah, and three reserved for presidential appointment. The distribution of seats had been the primary obstacle for opposition negotiators, who sought sufficient representation to block major legislative decisions. Their 11 allocated seats secure this veto authority.

In return for gaining this blocking power alongside a redrawing of electoral districts before next year's voting, Hezbollah committed to ending its prolonged sit-in demonstration, which had brought central Beirut to a standstill since late 2006. During his address, Sleiman thanked Qatar and the Arab League for their role in facilitating the settlement.

Sleiman emerged as the compromise choice, regarded by Lebanon's various political groups as an impartial figure—unlike prior presidents typically categorized as either pro-Syrian or pro-Western in orientation. During his decade leading the armed forces, Sleiman is credited with bringing together a previously fragmented military institution.

Nevertheless, he now leads a country still grappling with deep internal rifts. Lebanon's elected government, aligned with Western interests, has experienced prolonged tension with Hezbollah. Through public rhetoric and street demonstrations in recent years, Hezbollah signaled willingness to leverage its influence and popular support to topple the Sunni-dominated administration, raising concerns about renewed civil conflict that could further destabilize an already volatile region.

The presidential election marked the resolution of a crisis that had escalated into violent clashes earlier in the month. Tensions eased after the Lebanese government yielded to two central Hezbollah demands: rescinding a prohibition on Hezbollah's communications infrastructure and restoring the security chief at Beirut's airport to his position.

"The opposition's actions demonstrated this was not an attempted coup, but simply a push to reverse the government's two unlawful decisions," Nasrallah stated. He further pledged: "I guarantee that Hezbollah, Amal, and the Change and Reform bloc will not monopolize the opposition's Cabinet representation. We intend to allocate portions to other opposition factions—unfortunately, we must speak in terms of shares—even if this means reducing Hezbollah's own allocation."

Western nations, including the United States, have connected Hezbollah to multiple terrorist attacks targeting American, Israeli, and other Western interests, leading to its classification as a terrorist group by the U.S. government. Despite this designation, many across Lebanon and the broader Middle East, particularly within Shiite communities, regard Hezbollah fighters as freedom fighters rather than terrorists.

Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah declared his movement's full commitment to constructive participation in Lebanon's political future, striking a conciliatory tone just one day after parliament finally elected army commander Michel Sleiman as the country's new president. In remarks that signaled a shift toward national reconciliation, Nasrallah emphasized that Hezbollah sought genuine partnership in governance rather than any attempt to dominate or control state institutions, framing the movement's role as one of collaborative nation-building rather than sectarian assertion.

The presidential election itself marked the end of a prolonged and often tense political deadlock. Lebanon had been without a head of state for six months, during which parliament attempted and failed no fewer than nineteen times to elect a president, as rival political factions remained locked in disagreement over the country's leadership and the broader distribution of power. This extended vacancy at the highest level of government reflected the depth of Lebanon's political paralysis, leaving the presidency—a position reserved for a Maronite Christian under the country's confessional power-sharing system—unfilled and contributing to a broader sense of institutional drift.

The resolution of this impasse can be traced directly to a landmark agreement brokered in Doha, Qatar, where Lebanese political leaders from across the spectrum gathered to negotiate an end to eighteen months of escalating crisis. That crisis had brought Lebanon perilously close to renewed civil conflict, with sectarian tensions flaring and armed clashes erupting in Beirut and elsewhere, evoking painful memories of the country's devastating 1975-1990 civil war. The Doha talks succeeded where previous efforts had failed, producing a comprehensive power-sharing framework that addressed not only the presidential vacancy but also the broader question of how political authority would be distributed among Lebanon's competing factions.

Under the terms of this agreement, a consensus government was established featuring a carefully calibrated distribution of Cabinet seats. Portfolios were allocated among three distinct blocs: the parliamentary majority coalition, the opposition forces—which included Hezbollah and its allies—and nominees selected by the newly elected president himself. This tripartite division of ministerial positions was designed to ensure that no single faction could dominate the government while simultaneously guaranteeing that all major political currents in the country would have a meaningful stake in governance.

Nasrallah's statements following Sleiman's election were widely seen as an effort to reassure both domestic and international observers that Hezbollah, despite its considerable military and political power, intended to operate within the bounds of the new consensus arrangement rather than seeking to leverage its strength for unilateral advantage. His emphasis on partnership over domination appeared calculated to ease concerns about the movement's intentions as Lebanon embarked on this fragile new chapter, with many hoping that the Doha accord and the successful presidential election would pave the way for greater political stability after a period that had brought the small Mediterranean nation to the brink of renewed sectarian conflict.

Perched along the eastern shore of the Mediterranean Sea, Beirut has witnessed centuries of change, serving as a crossroads of cultures, religions, and civilizations.

counterfactuals.output:
# Nasrallah Hails Lebanese President's Election as 'National Victory' Following Doha Accord

**BEIRUT, Lebanon** — Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah addressed supporters Sunday in a televised speech celebrating the election of Michel Sleiman as Lebanon's president, calling the vote a milestone that ended nearly 18 months of political paralysis and brought the country back from the brink of wider conflict.

Sleiman, the former commander of the Lebanese Armed Forces, was elected by parliament earlier in the day, filling a presidency that had remained vacant since November 2007. His election was made possible by the Doha Agreement, a power-sharing deal brokered in the Qatari capital last week by Arab foreign ministers after Lebanon's worst internal violence since the 1975-1990 civil war.

"Today Lebanon has turned a page," Nasrallah told supporters via a large screen, as he continues to avoid public appearances citing security concerns. "What was achieved in Doha, and what we see today with the election of a president, is a victory for all the Lebanese people — not for one side against another."

## The Doha Agreement

The Doha talks were convened after clashes in early May between Hezbollah-led opposition fighters and government-aligned militias, which saw gunmen briefly seize control of predominantly Sunni neighborhoods in west Beirut. The violence, which killed more than 60 people, marked the most serious internal strife Lebanon had experienced in years and raised fears of a slide back into sectarian civil war.

Under the terms of the agreement, the rival parties agreed to:

- Elect Sleiman as a consensus president, ending the political vacuum
- Form a national unity government in which no single bloc holds a majority
- Adopt a new electoral law based on the 1960 framework for the next parliamentary elections

## Cabinet Allocation

Central to the Doha compromise was an agreement on the composition of the incoming Cabinet. Under the deal:

- The parliamentary majority, led by the Future Movement and its allies, will receive **16 seats**
- The opposition, including Hezbollah, Amal, and the Free Patriotic Movement, will hold **11 seats**
- President Sleiman will appoint the remaining **3 seats**

The formula effectively grants Hezbollah and its allies veto power over major government decisions, since 11 seats constitute a "blocking third" under Lebanon's constitutional requirements for key resolutions — a central demand of the opposition since the 2006 war with Israel.

Nasrallah addressed this arrangement directly in his remarks. "This is not about domination. It is about partnership," he said. "No single faction in Lebanon can again claim the right to decide the fate of this country alone."

## Reaction and Road Ahead

Saad Hariri, leader of the parliamentary majority, also welcomed Sleiman's election, calling it "a new beginning" for Lebanon, though tensions between the rival camps over the root causes of the crisis — including disputes over Hezbollah's weapons and a state telecommunications network — remain unresolved.

Sleiman, seen as a neutral figure acceptable to both the Western-backed majority and the Hezbollah-led opposition, now faces the task of forming a unity Cabinet under the new allocation and shepherding Lebanon toward parliamentary elections scheduled for 2009.

Analysts caution that while the Doha Agreement defused an immediate crisis, it did not resolve the deeper disputes over Hezbollah's armed status and Lebanon's political identity that have divided the country since the withdrawal of Syrian troops in 2005.

"Doha bought Lebanon time," said one Beirut-based political analyst. "Whether that time is used to build lasting institutions or simply to reset the clock until the next crisis remains to be seen."

*CNN's Beirut bureau contributed to this report.*

# Doha Agreement Ends Lebanon's Political Deadlock

**BEIRUT** — After 18 months of political paralysis that pushed Lebanon to the brink of renewed civil conflict, rival Lebanese factions reached a landmark power-sharing agreement in Doha, Qatar, bringing an end to one of the country's most severe political crises since the civil war.

## Background to the Crisis

The agreement followed a tense standoff between the Western-backed governing coalition and the Hezbollah-led opposition, a conflict that escalated dramatically in early May when Hezbollah fighters briefly seized control of parts of Beirut. The unprecedented show of force by the Shiite militant group and its allies underscored the severity of the deadlock and raised fears of a slide back into sectarian violence.

## The Doha Negotiations

Qatari mediators brought Lebanese leaders together for intensive talks aimed at resolving the underlying political disputes. The negotiations produced a comprehensive settlement addressing the presidency, electoral reforms, and — most contentiously — the composition of the national unity Cabinet.

## Cabinet Seat Distribution

Under the terms of the agreement, the new national unity government was structured as follows:

- **16 seats** allocated to the governing majority coalition
- **11 seats** allocated to the Hezbollah-led opposition
- **3 seats** allocated to the president, serving as a neutral arbiter between the factions

This formula notably granted the opposition — and by extension Hezbollah and its allies — effective veto power over major government decisions, a key demand that had fueled the prolonged crisis. The opposition had long insisted on "blocking third" representation, and the Doha formula secured this outcome.

## Hezbollah's Response

Hezbollah's leader, Sayyed Hassan Nasrallah, publicly welcomed the agreement, framing it as a vindication of the "sit-in" and broader pressure campaign his movement had waged. In remarks addressing supporters, Nasrallah declared that the outcome represented "a day of victory for all Lebanon," emphasizing that the deal validated the opposition's demands and restored what he characterized as a fairer balance of power within the state.

His comments were seen as an effort to project the settlement not as a compromise, but as a clear win for Hezbollah and its allies — reinforcing the movement's standing among its base while signaling reconciliation to the broader Lebanese public.

## Implications

The Doha Agreement was widely credited with pulling Lebanon back from the edge of a deeper conflict, restoring functioning government institutions, and setting the stage for the election of a new president. Analysts noted, however, that while the deal resolved the immediate crisis, it left unresolved the deeper structural tensions between Lebanon's sectarian factions — tensions that would continue to shape the country's fragile political landscape in the years that followed.

**Beirut, Lebanon** — Lebanon's parliament elected a new president Thursday, ending more than two years of political paralysis that left the country without a head of state amid one of the worst economic crises in its modern history. The election marks a significant breakthrough after more than a dozen failed attempts to fill the post, and comes with an unusual pledge of cooperation from Hezbollah, the powerful Iran-backed movement that had long been blamed by rivals for obstructing the process.

## A Long-Awaited Vote

Lebanon's presidency, reserved for a Christian under the country's sectarian power-sharing system, had sat empty since the previous officeholder's term expired, plunging the nation into a constitutional limbo that paralyzed government decision-making even as Lebanon grappled with currency collapse, banking sector implosion, and the lingering aftermath of the 2020 Beirut port explosion.

Repeated parliamentary sessions to elect a successor collapsed for lack of quorum or failure to reach the required majority, as rival blocs — broadly split along the lines of Hezbollah and its allies versus a loose coalition of its opponents — refused to back one another's candidates. The stalemate reflected deeper fractures in Lebanese politics, where the presidency has become both a symbolic prize and a practical lever of influence over the government, the military, and foreign policy direction.

Thursday's vote succeeded after backroom negotiations produced a consensus candidate acceptable to enough factions to clear the two-thirds quorum required in an initial round, and the simple majority needed for final passage. Lawmakers and diplomats described the breakthrough as the product of sustained regional and international pressure, including from Saudi Arabia, France, and the United States, all of which had pushed rival Lebanese factions toward compromise.

## Hezbollah Signals a Shift

In a notable statement following the vote, Hezbollah — the Shiite militant group and political party that maintains the country's most formidable armed force outside the state — pledged to cooperate with the new president and support efforts to form a functioning government. The group's leadership has historically wielded outsized influence over presidential selection, given its parliamentary bloc and alliance with the Free Patriotic Movement, one of Lebanon's largest Christian parties.

Hezbollah officials framed the pledge as a commitment to national stability, with a senior figure stating the group would not stand in the way of consensus-building and would engage constructively with the incoming administration on matters of governance and economic recovery.

Analysts cautioned that Hezbollah's cooperative posture likely reflects calculated interests rather than a fundamental shift in its regional agenda. The group remains under intense scrutiny over its military capabilities, its role in regional conflicts tied to Iran, and its influence over Lebanese state institutions — issues that have repeatedly put it at odds with rival Sunni political factions and their international backers.

## The Sunni-Hezbollah Power Struggle

The presidential vacancy cannot be understood outside the broader struggle for power between Hezbollah and Lebanon's Sunni political establishment, a rivalry that has shaped the country's politics for nearly two decades.

Tensions trace back to the assassination of former Prime Minister Rafik Hariri in 2005, a Sunni leader whose killing was widely attributed — including by a UN-backed tribunal — to Hezbollah operatives, a charge the group has always denied. Hariri's death triggered mass protests and the withdrawal of Syrian troops from Lebanon after nearly three decades of occupation, but it also hardened a political divide between the Hariri-aligned March 14 coalition, backed by Saudi Arabia and Western powers, and the Hezbollah-led March 8 alliance, backed by Syria and Iran.

Since then, the two camps have repeatedly clashed over control of the presidency, the cabinet, and key security portfolios. The rivalry escalated into open street violence in 2008, when Hezbollah fighters briefly seized parts of predominantly Sunni West Beirut after the government moved against the group's telecommunications network — a episode many Sunnis viewed as a watershed moment demonstrating Hezbollah's willingness to turn its weapons inward.

The Sunni community's traditional leadership, long centered on the Hariri family and the Future Movement, has itself been in disarray in recent years amid Saudi Arabia's reduced patronage and Saad Hariri's on-again, off-again retreat from politics, leaving a leadership vacuum that has complicated Sunni efforts to counterbalance Hezbollah's influence.

Meanwhile, Hezbollah has only grown more entrenched, citing its role in fighting Israel and the Islamic State as justification for retaining its weapons despite domestic and international calls for the group to disarm under UN Security Council Resolution 1701. Critics argue Hezbollah's arsenal — larger than the Lebanese army's in some estimates — has effectively given it veto power over major state decisions, including the presidency itself, since no president can realistically govern without some accommodation with the group.

## What Comes Next

The election of a new president is expected to pave the way for the formation of a new government, a process that itself is likely to be contentious given the same sectarian and factional divisions that produced the vacancy. Lebanon's international partners, including the International Monetary Fund, have made further financial assistance contingent on the country completing long-delayed reforms, many of which require functioning executive institutions.

Whether Hezbollah's pledge of cooperation translates into genuine power-sharing or merely a tactical pause in the broader contest for influence remains to be seen. For a country whose institutions have repeatedly buckled under the weight of factional rivalry, Thursday's vote offers a rare moment of political movement — but few in Beirut are treating it as a resolution to the deeper struggle over who ultimately governs Lebanon.
